title: Why isn't the shop paid the moment you tap your card?

cards.title: You tap, it beeps, and you walk away.
cards.text: Tapping your card feels like paying. But the card reader only sends a short message asking your bank if this card can pay.
cards.hook: So where does that message go before it comes back with a yes?

notes: The reader sends a short message: can this card pay?

cards.title: The message goes to the shop's bank, then a card network, then your bank
cards.text: The reader's message reaches the shop's bank. That bank passes it to a card network, a company such as Visa or Mastercard that links banks. The network passes it to your bank, which answers yes or no. The answer travels back the same way, in a couple of seconds.
cards.hook: So when your bank says yes, does the shop get the money?

notes: The message goes to the shop's bank, then a card network, then your bank
The yes comes back the same way

cards.title: Your bank's yes is a promise to pay, and the money hasn't reached the shop yet
cards.text: Your bank checks that the card is real and that you have enough money or credit. If so, it takes that amount off what you can spend straight away. So you can't spend the same money twice. But the money hasn't reached the shop yet.
cards.hook: So why does the shop have to wait to be paid?

notes: This is what you can spend
The yes takes the amount off what you can spend
The money hasn't reached the shop yet

cards.title: Banks move money in totals, so the shop is usually paid a few working days later
cards.text: Banks don't move money for every single tap. They gather many payments and add them up, and the shop's bank is paid in totals. So the shop is usually paid a few working days after your tap.
cards.takeaway: The yes comes back in seconds, and the shop is usually paid a few working days later.

notes: Banks add many payments up into totals
A few working days later the totals reach the shop

cards.note: The shop gets a little less than you paid, because a small fee is shared among your bank, the card network and the shop's bank. The fee that goes to your bank is called the interchange fee.
